subject: English
text: The Last Lesson by Alphonse Daudet is set in Alsace (France) during the Franco-Prussian War, after Prussia captured Alsace and Lorraine. A Prussian order bans French; German must now be taught. The narrator Franz, who often skipped lessons, arrives late and finds a solemn class. His teacher M. Hamel, dressed in his fine clothes, announces this is their last French lesson. Franz suddenly regrets not learning French and finds the grammar easy when he pays attention. M. Hamel says French is the most beautiful and logical language and urges them to guard it, as it is the key to their identity and freedom. Theme: the importance of one's language and mother tongue, the pain of losing freedom, and the value of not procrastinating. It ends with M. Hamel writing 'Vive La France!' on the board.

subject: English
text: Lost Spring by Anees Jung has two parts. Part 1 'Sometimes I Find a Rupee in the Garbage' is about Saheb-e-Alam, a ragpicker from Seemapuri (a Delhi slum, migrants from Bangladesh). For these children garbage is gold, a means of survival. Saheb later works at a tea stall, losing his freedom. Part 2 'I Want to Drive a Car' is about Mukesh of Firozabad, the centre of India's glass-blowing (bangle) industry, where families are trapped in poverty for generations, working in dangerous conditions that harm their eyes. Mukesh dreams of being a motor mechanic, daring to break the tradition. Themes: child labour, poverty, exploitation, the vicious circle of caste/tradition, and lost childhood dreams.

subject: English
text: Deep Water by William Douglas describes how the author overcame his fear of water. As a child he had a fright at a beach; later a bigger boy threw him into the deep end of a YMCA pool, where he nearly drowned and developed a lasting terror of water. This fear spoiled his enjoyment of activities. As an adult he hired an instructor who trained him piece by piece over months until he could swim, then he tested himself in lakes to conquer the last traces of fear. Theme: fear must be faced and defeated; 'All we have to fear is fear itself.' Determination and willpower can overcome deep-rooted terror.

subject: English
text: The Rattrap by Selma Lagerlof is about a poor peddler who sells rattraps and believes the whole world is a giant rattrap that baits people with riches and comforts. After stealing money from an old crofter who befriended him, he hides in a forest and feels trapped. He is mistaken by an ironmaster for an old regiment comrade and invited home. The ironmaster's kind daughter Edla treats him warmly despite knowing the truth. Her kindness transforms him; he leaves the stolen money to be returned and a rattrap as a gift, signing as Captain von Stahle, redeemed by being treated as a good human. Theme: essential human goodness can be awakened by kindness, love, and understanding.

subject: English
text: Indigo by Louis Fischer (from his biography of Gandhi) describes Gandhi's 1917 Champaran movement in Bihar. Sharecropping peasants were forced by British planters to grow indigo on 15 percent of their land and hand it over as rent (the tinkathia system). When synthetic dye reduced indigo's value, planters demanded compensation to release peasants. Gandhi investigated, was ordered to leave but refused, courting arrest, which rallied the peasants. Through civil disobedience and negotiation he won a 25 percent refund and, more importantly, taught peasants courage and self-reliance. Themes: nonviolent resistance (satyagraha), self-reliance, freeing people from fear, and India's freedom struggle at the grassroots.

subject: English
text: Poets and Pancakes by Asokamitran is a humorous account of Gemini Studios (a major film studio in Chennas/Madras). 'Pancake' was the brand of make-up used. The essay describes the make-up department (people of many communities), the office boy who aspired to be an actor/poet, the legal adviser who accidentally ended an actress's career, and the visits of an English poet (Stephen Spender) and a group called MRA (Moral Re-Armament). It gently satirises the workings, hierarchies, and eccentric people of the studio. Themes: the world of Indian cinema, human ambition and frustration, and light satire on office politics.

subject: English
text: The Interview by Christopher Silvester has two parts. Part 1 discusses the interview as a modern art form: opinions differ — some see it as a source of truth and a valuable art, while some celebrities dislike it, feeling it intrudes and 'diminishes' them (Rudyard Kipling, V.S. Naipaul disliked interviews). Part 2 is Mukund Padmanabhan's interview of the famous writer Umberto Eco, who explains his 'interstices' theory (using empty moments productively) and how he writes scholarly work, essays, and novels (like The Name of the Rose). Theme: the value, ethics, and technique of interviews, and insight into a creative mind.

subject: English
text: Going Places by A.R. Barton is about Sophie, an adolescent girl from a lower-middle-class family who dreams beyond her means — of owning a boutique, becoming an actress or a fashion designer. She fantasises about meeting Danny Casey, a young Irish football star, and even claims to have met him, though it is imaginary. Her friend Jansie is realistic and knows they are destined for the biscuit factory. Sophie waits for Casey who never comes, then imagines the meeting. Theme: adolescent fantasy versus reality, the escapism of dreams, and the gap between aspiration and one's actual circumstances.

subject: English
text: My Mother at Sixty-Six by Kamala Das. Driving to Cochin airport, the poet sees her aged mother dozing, her face 'ashen like that of a corpse', and is struck by the fear of losing her (fear of death and separation). To push away the painful thought she looks outside at young trees 'sprinting' and merry children (images of youth and life, contrasting old age). At the airport, the old familiar ache and childhood fear return; she smiles and only says, 'see you soon, Amma,' hiding her pain. Poetic devices: simile ('like a corpse', 'as a late winter's moon'), imagery, contrast. Theme: the pain of ageing parents, filial love, and the fear of separation.

subject: English
text: Keeping Quiet by Pablo Neruda urges a moment of silence and stillness. If everyone counts to twelve and keeps still, without rushing or speaking any language, there would be a sudden strange feeling of togetherness. This silence would let fishermen not harm whales, and the man gathering salt to look at his hurt hands — a pause from harmful activity. The poet clarifies this stillness is not total inactivity or death; it is introspection to end wars of aggression against ourselves and nature. The Earth teaches this, seeming dead in winter yet alive. Theme: the value of introspection, self-examination, universal brotherhood, peace, and rejecting violence.

subject: English
text: A Thing of Beauty by John Keats (from Endymion) opens with the famous line 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever.' Its beauty increases and never fades into nothingness; it gives us a quiet bower (shelter) and sweet sleep full of health and peaceful breathing. Despite gloom, despondency, and the lack of noble natures, beautiful things remove the pall (covering) from our dark spirits. Examples of beauty: the sun, moon, trees, daffodils, clear streams, and forests. These are like an 'endless fountain of immortal drink' pouring from heaven. Theme: beauty is a permanent source of joy that lifts human suffering and connects us to nature and the divine.

subject: English
text: A Roadside Stand by Robert Frost is about the poor rural people who set up a small roadside stand to sell produce, hoping for city money to support their lives. The polished, indifferent city traffic mostly speeds past, annoyed or unmoved, offering no trade. The poet criticises how 'greedy good-doers' and authorities exploit these people with false promises of a better life while actually taking away their peace of mind. He feels the pathos of their unfulfilled longing and childlike hope. Theme: rural poverty, the neglect and exploitation of the poor by the city and the state, and the wide gap between rich and poor.

subject: English
text: Aunt Jennifer's Tigers by Adrienne Rich. Aunt Jennifer embroiders bright, fearless, prancing tigers on a screen — 'denizens of a world of green', chivalric and confident, unafraid of men. In contrast, her own fingers flutter and the 'massive weight of Uncle's wedding band' sits heavily on her hand, showing she is oppressed and burdened by a male-dominated marriage. Even when she dies, her 'terrified hands' will still be 'ringed with ordeals'. But the tigers she made will go on prancing, proud and free. Theme: the oppression of women in a patriarchal society, and how art can express a longing for the freedom denied in real life.

subject: English
text: The Third Level by Jack Finney is a psychological story blending reality and fantasy. Charley, a New York commuter, claims to have discovered a mysterious 'third level' at Grand Central Station (which really has only two) that is a gateway to 1894 — a peaceful past with old-style clothes, gaslights, and cheaper prices. He wants to buy tickets to Galesburg (a calm town) to escape the stress and insecurity of modern life. His psychiatrist calls it a 'waking-dream wish fulfilment' (escapism). Later Charley finds an old letter from his friend Sam who apparently reached 1894. Theme: escapism from the anxiety and insecurity of modern life into an idealised past.

subject: English
text: The Tiger King by Kalki is a satire. The Maharaja of Pratibandapuram, called the Tiger King, is told at birth by astrologers that his death will come from a tiger (the hundredth one). To defy fate, he vows to kill a hundred tigers and bans tiger hunting by anyone else. He kills 99, marries to hunt in another state, and struggles to find the hundredth. Finally a tiger is brought; he 'kills' it, but it only faints and is actually killed by his men. Ironically, he dies from a splinter in a cheap wooden toy tiger he bought for his son's birthday — the 'hundredth tiger'. Theme: satire on the vanity, arrogance, and whims of autocratic rulers, and the futility of trying to defeat destiny.

subject: English
chapter: Vistas: Journey to the End of the Earth
text: Journey to the End of the Earth by Tishani Doshi records the author's voyage to Antarctica on the 'Students on Ice' programme, which takes students to the ends of the Earth to raise environmental awareness. Antarctica, once part of the giant landmass Gondwana, holds Earth's history in its ice and shows the impact of human activity — global warming, the depleting ozone, melting ice caps. Small organisms like phytoplankton at the base of the food chain reveal how small changes have huge effects. Theme: climate change, the need for environmental conservation, the interconnectedness of ecosystems, and learning from the past to save the future.

subject: English
text: The Enemy by Pearl S. Buck is set in Japan during World War II. Dr Sadao Hoki, a skilled Japanese surgeon, finds a wounded American prisoner of war (the enemy) washed ashore. Torn between patriotism/law and his duty as a doctor, he and his wife Hana operate on and shelter the man, risking being labelled traitors. Their servants leave in protest. Sadao informs a General (his patient) who promises to send assassins, but they never come. Finally Sadao helps the American, Tom, escape to a nearby island with supplies. Theme: humanism transcends national enmity; the conflict between professional/ethical duty and prejudice; and the triumph of compassion over hatred.

subject: English
text: Should Wizard Hit Mommy? by John Updike explores a child's questioning mind. Every day Jo (Joanne), a four-year-old, listens to her father Jack's bedtime stories about a creature named Roger (Skunk, Chipmunk, etc.). In the story, a bad-smelling Roger Skunk is teased, so a wizard gives him a nice smell; but his mother is angry and hits the wizard, insisting he restore the natural (bad) smell so the child stays as God/nature made him. Jo objects — she wants the wizard to hit the mommy, believing the nice smell was better. Jack refuses to change the ending. Theme: the conflict between a child's sense of individuality/change and an adult's insistence on convention and acceptance; the difference between a child's and an adult's worldview.

subject: English
chapter: Vistas: On the Face of It
text: On the Face of It by Susan Hill is a play about overcoming the sense of loss due to physical disfigurement. Derry, a young boy with a burnt, scarred face, feels rejected and bitter, avoiding people. He enters the garden of Mr Lamb, an old man with a tin (artificial) leg who is also mocked ('Lamey-Lamb') but lives cheerfully, welcoming everyone and finding beauty in weeds and life. Mr Lamb's positive outlook inspires Derry to see beyond his scar and value himself. Derry returns, but tragically finds Mr Lamb has fallen from a ladder and died. Theme: physical disability matters less than attitude; the pain of isolation, the power of friendship and a positive outlook on life.

subject: English
text: Evans Tries an O-Level by Colin Dexter is a witty crime/prison story. Evans, a clever and cunning prisoner (nicknamed 'Evans the Break' for his escapes), asks to sit an O-Level German exam in his cell. Despite tight security by the Governor, Evans executes an elaborate escape plan with outside help — a fake invigilator, a planted question paper with instructions, and disguises. He fakes being injured, and after appearing to be recaptured, cleverly slips away again using the very officials meant to catch him. Theme: cleverness, meticulous planning, and the humorous outwitting of authority; appearances can be deceptive.

subject: English
text: Memories of Childhood presents two autobiographical extracts by women from marginalised communities. Part 1 'The Cutting of My Long Hair' by Zitkala-Sa (a Native American) recalls the humiliation at a carlisle boarding school where her culture was suppressed and her long hair was forcibly cut, symbolising loss of identity and dignity. Part 2 'We Too are Human Beings' by Bama (a Tamil Dalit) recalls how as a child she first realised untouchability and caste discrimination, then resolved to study hard and rise above it. Theme: the pain of social discrimination (racism and casteism), oppression of marginalised people, and the strength to resist and reclaim dignity through education.

subject: English
text: A notice is a formal written communication that informs a group of people about an event, meeting, competition, lost/found item, etc. Format (usually in a box): NAME OF ORGANISATION/SCHOOL at the top, the word NOTICE, a heading/title, the date of writing, the body (giving all details — what, when, where, who, why, how, whom to contact), and at the end the writer's name and designation (e.g. Secretary, Head Boy). Keep it short (about 50 words), factual, and impersonal (third person). Use the 5 Ws and 1 H to cover all information. Marks are given for format, content, and expression.

subject: English
text: Classified advertisements are short advertisements grouped by category in newspapers (e.g. Situation Vacant, To Let, For Sale, Lost and Found, Matrimonial). They are brief and to the point, usually written in a box, in a telegraphic style using abbreviations to save space. Include: the category heading, essential details (item/service, condition, price, contact number/address), and be concise (about 50 words). Commercial (display) advertisements are larger, use catchy slogans, pictures, and persuasive language to promote a product or event. Focus on clarity, relevance of details, and correct format for marks.

subject: English
chapter: Writing Skills: Posters, Invitations and Replies
text: A poster is a visual formal message to create awareness or invite people to an event/cause. It includes a catchy title/slogan, the issue, essential details (date, time, venue), the issuing authority, and often a call to action; it uses attractive layout, though content is what earns marks. Invitations are of two types: formal (printed, third person, no signature, box format — for weddings, functions) and informal (letter form, first person, personal tone). Replies to invitations may be formal (accept/decline in third person) or informal (a warm personal note). Keep invitations concise with the occasion, date, time, and venue clearly stated.

subject: English
chapter: Writing Skills: Formal Letters (Application and Complaint)
text: Formal letters follow a fixed format: sender's address, date, receiver's address/designation, subject line, salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), body (in clear paragraphs), complimentary close (Yours faithfully/sincerely), and the sender's name. Types: (1) Letters to the editor (raising public issues), (2) Application letters — job applications with a covering letter and bio-data/resume, (3) Complaint letters — clearly state the problem, relevant details (date, bill/order number), the inconvenience caused, and the action/redress expected, in a polite but firm tone, (4) Enquiry and order/placement letters. Keep the tone formal and impersonal; be clear, concise, and courteous. Marks are for format, content, fluency, and accuracy.

subject: English
text: An article is a piece of writing expressing the writer's views/opinions on a topic of interest to a wide audience. Format: a suitable Title (centred), the writer's name (By-line) below it, followed by the body. Structure the body into: an introduction (introduce the topic, catch attention), the main body (2-3 paragraphs with points, causes, effects, examples, arguments), and a conclusion (suggestions/solutions and a closing thought). Use a formal, coherent style, appropriate vocabulary, and connectors. Word limit is usually about 120-150 words. Marks are awarded for format (title + by-line), content (relevant ideas), expression, and grammatical accuracy.

subject: English
text: A report is a formal factual account of an event, function, or situation (e.g. a school function, an accident, a survey). Format: a Heading/Title, the reporter's name (by-line, e.g. 'by ABC, Staff Reporter'), place and date, followed by the body. The body is written in the past tense and third person (impersonal), covering what happened, when, where, who was involved, and the outcome, in a logical order. It should be factual and objective (no personal opinion), concise, and structured into paragraphs. Types include newspaper reports and reports for a magazine/school. Word limit about 120-150 words. Marks are for format, content, and expression.
